inputs.label: Requirements in the repo
inputs.detail: Product-approved feature requirements, acceptance criteria, and relevant validation cases.

inputs.label: TDD-prepared target plan
inputs.detail: Planned implementation units, source paths, spec paths, mappings, and concrete assertions.

inputs.label: Repo + NFR patterns

red-green-refactor.title: The engineer–Codex working loop.
red-green-refactor.purpose: Show where most implementation iteration happens and why green is a checkpoint rather than a PR-ready finish line.
red-green-refactor.teachingPoint: For unit-testable behavior already in approved scope, update Jest first and confirm red before changing product code; surface genuinely new behavior as a potential gap for review.
red-green-refactor.headline: GREEN IS A CHECKPOINT. KEEP LEARNING.

canonicalMethodology.label: Canonical TDD methodology
canonicalMethodology.testList: List the desired behaviors, then choose exactly one case at a time.

cycle.definition: Turn one behavior into a runnable test and confirm it fails in the expected way.
Write just enough code for the new test and every earlier test to pass.
While all tests remain green, improve the design without changing behavior.

canonicalMethodology.repeat: Choose the next behavior from the list and repeat until the list is empty.

validatorGovernance.label: Validator evidence around the loop
validatorGovernance.statement: The validator does not redefine Red, Green, or Refactor.
validatorGovernance.boundary: Approvals, baselines, traceability, drift checks, and the composed gate are governance around TDD; they are not canonical color definitions.

workingLoop.collaboration: The engineer and Codex iterate one reviewed behavior or slice at a time.
workingLoop.greenCheckpoint: Passing Jest tests are a safe checkpoint for local exploratory testing, not proof that the feature is PR-ready.
workingLoop.localValidation: Exercise the local build to find incorrect behavior, UX defects, and edge cases that unit checks alone may not reveal.
workingLoop.inScopeChange: For a unit-testable behavior change already covered by approved requirements, update the Jest evidence first, confirm the expected failure, and then change product code.
workingLoop.outsideScopeChange: Record behavior outside approved requirements as a potential gap; do not implement it opportunistically.
workingLoop.refactor: Improve structure only while the suite remains green, then repeat until the complete reviewed slice is ready.

narration.text: This is where engineers and Codex spend most of their time together. Choose one planned behavior. Red: write its requirement-backed test and confirm the expected failure. Green: make the smallest change that gets it—and earlier tests—passing. Green is a checkpoint, not proof that the feature is PR-ready. Run the feature locally and explore behavior, UX, and edge cases. For a unit-testable change already in approved scope, update Jest first, confirm red, then change the code. New behavior outside that boundary becomes a potential gap for review. Refactor while green; repeat until the slice is ready.

narration.text: Meet the TDD Jest Validation Gate. Here's the code-first risk: Codex writes the change, then tests its own output. Those tests can pass while simply mirroring the implementation. TDD flips it: requirement-backed tests define the boundary and drive code. Unmapped implementation surfaces as drift or a potential gap. SDD phase four sits between reviewed planning and product code. Engineers and Codex stay inside the boundary. After implementation, Playwright tests browser journeys. It complements, not replaces, Jest. The skill turns intent into auditable evidence. It maps requirement and acceptance IDs to Jest specs, ties specs to source paths, and records the baseline. It detects implementation drift and weakened tests, combining traceability, test integrity, and feature readiness in one gate. Begin with product-approved requirements committed to the repo. Ask the TDD phase to prepare the Unit Test Target Plan, mapping units to source paths, specs, and assertions. Review and approve the plan, then one representative failing spec. Generate the planned suite, capture the red-phase baseline, and run the gate before changing product code. This is where engineers and Codex spend most of their time together. Choose one planned behavior. Red: write its requirement-backed test and confirm the expected failure. Green: make the smallest change that gets it—and earlier tests—passing. Green is a checkpoint, not proof that the feature is PR-ready. Run the feature locally and explore behavior, UX, and edge cases. For a unit-testable change already in approved scope, update Jest first, confirm red, then change the code. New behavior outside that boundary becomes a potential gap for review. Refactor while green; repeat until the slice is ready. The dashboard turns the audit into decisions. What blocks the gate? Which requirements have evidence? Which tests need mappings? Are the plan and baseline present? Were tests deleted or weakened? Which potential gaps need review? The numbers change; these questions remain useful. Use it in Codex, from the CLI, or through SDD Orchestrator, with human approval at key checkpoints. Try it on your next feature, evaluate the evidence, and stress-test the guardrails. Then contribute prompts, checks, tests, and dashboard metrics for the next engineer.
